Test overdispersion in a fitted count model

Source: R/overdispersion_test.R
mysterycall_overdispersion_test.Rd

Computes the Pearson chi-square dispersion statistic (phi = chi-sq / residual df) for any fitted count model and returns a plain-language interpretation. The calculation mirrors the overdisp_fun() approach used in the mystery-caller Rmd analyses: Pearson residuals are squared and summed, divided by the residual degrees of freedom, and tested against a chi-square distribution.

Usage

mysterycall_overdispersion_test(
  model,
  phi_thresholds = c(mild = 1.2, moderate = 1.5, severe = 2),
  digits = 3L
)

Arguments

model

A fitted model object. Supported classes:

glmerMod

From lme4::glmer().

glm

From stats::glm().

negbin

From MASS::glm.nb().

Any object that responds to residuals() with type = "pearson" and to df.residual() is also accepted.

phi_thresholds

Named numeric vector. Boundaries used to assign the verbal interpretation category. Must have names "mild", "moderate", and "severe" and must satisfy mild < moderate < severe. Default: c(mild = 1.2, moderate = 1.5, severe = 2.0).

digits

Integer. Number of decimal places for phi and the p-value in formatted output. Default 3L.

Value

A list of class "mysterycall_overdispersion_test" with elements:

phi

Numeric. Pearson dispersion ratio (chi-sq / df).

pearson_chisq

Numeric. Raw Pearson chi-square statistic.

df

Integer. Residual degrees of freedom.

p_value

Numeric. P-value from pchisq(pearson_chisq, df, lower.tail = FALSE).

p_fmt

Character. Formatted p-value (e.g. "<0.001").

interpretation

Character. One-sentence verbal category.

recommendation

Character. One-sentence action sentence.

sentence

Character. Combined summary sentence suitable for inline reporting.

Details

This is the standalone export of the overdispersion check that mysterycall_poisson_model() performs internally. Use it to diagnose any fitted count model after fitting — including negative binomial models, where phi near 1.0 confirms that the dispersion was adequately absorbed.

Interpretation thresholds

phi < 1.0

Underdispersion — the model may overfit.

1.0 <= phi < 1.2

No significant overdispersion.

1.2 <= phi < 1.5

Mild overdispersion.

1.5 <= phi < 2.0

Moderate overdispersion.

phi >= 2.0

Severe overdispersion.

Mixed-effects caveat

For mixed-effects models (glmmTMB, merMod), df.residual() counts only the fixed-effect parameters and ignores the effective degrees of freedom consumed by the random effects, so phi is an approximation rather than an exact dispersion ratio. The verbal interpretation accounts for this by treating low residual phi as expected for negative-binomial and mixed models (dispersion absorbed by the NB variance or random intercepts) rather than as overfitting. For a formal simulation-based check on a GLMM, prefer DHARMa::testDispersion().

Examples

## Poisson GLM on count data ------------------------------------------------
set.seed(42)
n   <- 200
dat <- data.frame(
  y   = rpois(n, lambda = exp(0.5 + 0.3 * rnorm(n))),
  x1  = rnorm(n),
  grp = sample(c("A", "B"), n, replace = TRUE)
)
fit <- glm(y ~ x1 + grp, data = dat, family = poisson())
result <- mysterycall_overdispersion_test(fit)
print(result)
#> Pearson dispersion phi=1.240 (chi-sq=244, df=197, p=0.012): Mild overdispersion (phi=1.240). Negative binomial model may improve fit. 
#> Consider fitting a negative binomial model with mysterycall_nb_model() to improve standard-error estimates. 

## Gaussian GLM (non-count, shows underdispersion path) ---------------------
fit2 <- glm(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mtcars, family = gaussian())
mysterycall_overdispersion_test(fit2)
#> Pearson dispersion phi=6.592 (chi-sq=191, df=29, p=<0.001): Severe overdispersion (phi=6.592). Negative binomial or zero-inflated model strongly recommended. 
#> Switch to a negative binomial or zero-inflated negative binomial model immediately; Poisson standard errors are severely underestimated.
